title: How To Determine Your Personal Savings Rate (U.S. Formula)
description: The metric that matters more than income or net worth.
content:
Net Worth is a vanity metric; it tells you how you did in the past. Income is a vanity metric; it tells you how much flows through you. **Savings Rate** is the only metric that predicts when you will be free. It measures the gap between your income and your ego. A person earning $50k and saving 50% will retire decades before a person earning $500k and saving 5%. This guide provides the standard formula to calculate this number and benchmarks to aim for.

Key Takeaways

  • The Formula: (Total Savings / Gross Income). Total Savings includes 401k (yours + match), IRA, HSA, and cash savings. Gross Income includes your salary + employer match.
  • Principal Payments: Paying down mortgage principal increases Net Worth, but it is not 'liquid savings'. Most strict FIRE definitions exclude it from the Savings Rate calculation.
  • The Benchmarks: 5% (Average American). 15% (Standard Retirement at 65). 25% (Retire Early / Wealthy). 50% (FIRE in 15 years).
  • Lead vs Lag: Savings Rate is a 'Leading Indicator'. If you fix this number today, your Net Worth must rise tomorrow.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US average savings rate fluctuates between 3% and 6%. This is dangerously low given the cost of healthcare in retirement. Tracking this number monthly gamifies the process of wealth building.

Running the Numbers

Example: Annual Salary $100,000. Employer Match $4,000.

The Numerator (Savings)

  • Employee 401k: $10,000.
  • Employer Match: $4,000.
  • Roth IRA: $7,000.
  • Cash to HYSA: $3,000.
  • Total Saved: $24,000.

The Denominator (Income)

  • Salary: $100,000.
  • Employer Match: $4,000.
  • Total Income: $104,000.

The Result

$24,000 / $104,000 = 23% Savings Rate.
Verdict: Excellent. You are on track to retire early (mid-50s).

How to Hack the Rate

  1. The 'Anti-Budget': Focus only on this number. If you hit a 25% savings rate, you can guilt-free spend the other 75%. You don't need to track lattes.
  2. Bank the Raise: When you get a 10% raise, increase your savings by 10%. Your lifestyle stays the same, but your rate jumps. This is the 'painless' path.
  3. Gross vs Net: Some people use Net Income (take-home). This yields a higher percentage (e.g., 40%). Just be consistent. We prefer Gross because it includes the tax burden you are managing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does debt payoff count?

Paying interest? No. Paying principal? Technically yes (increases Net Worth), but for retirement planning, it's safer to exclude it. Cash flow is king.

What is a 'good' rate?

20% is the gold standard. It creates a massive buffer for life's errors.

How do I track this?

Spreadsheet. Update it once a month. Seeing the percentage tick up from 12% to 13% is incredibly motivating.
